title: Degraded paths and graceful routing decision tree for deployment modes
content:
Purpose
This note captures an operational decision tree and pragmatic guidance for routing requests across Redwood’s Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes during steady-state and degraded conditions. It focuses on isolation boundaries, control plane decisioning, and multi-region fallback patterns — oriented around what oncall and platform teams need to do when things deviate from normal.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to control-plane routing (API frontend -> model runtime selection) and data-plane routing (egress, region selection).
- Assumes model variants are tagged by compatibility (e.g., v1, v1-quant, v1-fallback) and by performance profile.
- SLA tiers: "platinum" customers on Dedicated, "standard" on Hosted. Private deployments have customer-managed control plane, limited Redwood visibility.
- Key goals during degraded state: preserve safety (no data leakage), meet latency SLO where possible, avoid cascading outages.

High-level patterns (short)
- Hosted: Centralized control plane, global routing decisions with awareness of capacity and regional load. Default fallback = alternate hosted model variant or cross-region route. Isolation: logical tenant isolation with shared runtime pools.
- Dedicated: Tenant-dedicated pools. Control plane still central but routing constrained by tenant capacity and dedicated resource affinity. Isolation: compute + storage isolated; control-plane can perform shadow/telemetry but must not redirect tenant data to other tenants.
- Private: Customer-managed control plane or partial control plane. Redwood's recommended routing guidance is advisory; any automatic fallback that touches customer-managed networks must be opted-in. Isolation: strongest (physical/network), fewer cross-tenant options.

Decision tree (operational) - top level
1) Detect: Trigger type (latency spike, model OOMs, region outage, control plane partition). Identify scope: single-tenant, multi-tenant subset, global.
2) Containment: If tenant-specific and Dedicated or Private, restrict actions to that tenant’s routing domain. If Hosted and multi-tenant, consider global mitigations.
3) Route selection: Evaluate in this order (can be configured per-customer):
   a) Local: same region, same model variant on hot cache.
   b) Local fallback: same region, compatible lower-cost variant (quantized or smaller).
   c) Regional failover: different region same cloud provider, respect data residency tags.
   d) Cross-cloud fallback: only for customers who opted-in and when region failover exhausted.
   e) Queue/backpressure: reject or queue requests for a tenant with explicit retry-after if no allowed fallback.
4) Notify and escalate: Push an event to Ops channel; if SLA risk, page SRE.

Routing rules nuance by deployment mode
- Hosted:
  - Smart routing broker keeps global view of capacity and will choose between region-local and region-remote based on predicted tail latency and token-cost budget.
  - Default behavior: allow model variant fallback but do not change data egress region unless customer allows (privacy/policy).
  - Graceful degradation: automatic per-tenant prefix caching and request-level hints (score-based) reduce load; if degraded, reduce max output tokens to preserve throughput.

- Dedicated:
  - Tenant has reserved pools; routing must honor capacity reservations. Control plane will not route tenant work to other tenant-dedicated pools.
  - Allowed mitigations: shift traffic to tenant’s burst capacity, short-lived spill to compatible shared overflow pools if contract allows (explicit opt-in).
  - When dedicated pool is partially degraded (OOMs), the decision tree prefers local fallback model and throttling; only allow overflow if signed SLA/contract permits.

- Private:
  - Redwood prefers advisory configuration pushed to customer control plane. Any automatic cross-network failover should be explicitly configured in the customer onboarding profile.
  - Logging and telemetry collection limited by customer settings (may delay detection).
  - If the customer control plane is unreachable, Redwood falls back to documented noop mode: return 503 with clear error and store events for later sync.

Isolation boundaries checklist
- Data sovereignty: do not change egress location unless customer model policy allows. Mark tenants with "no-cross-region-egress" and enforce in broker.
- Tenant compute isolation: Dedicated pools must be never used for other tenants except approved overflow; enforce via entitlements policy.
- Control plane access: Private deployments may restrict control-plane operations; treat all control-plane mutations as sensitive and require RBAC and audit logs.

Operational play: sample degraded scenario and steps
Scenario A: Hosted, region A experiencing GPU node failures -> increased latency and token drops.
- Detection: Platform telemetry triggers region latency threshold.
- Immediate mitigations (automated): reduce batching window for region A, enable prefix-KV cache hits only, limit max tokens returned per request by 30%.
- Control plane decisions: redirect new requests to region B if tenant allows cross-region; otherwise attempt local fallback model variant (quantized).
- If cross-region used: tag requests with egress_notice and set customer-facing header explaining possible region change.
- Follow-up: after stabilizing, run health-checks before gradually rolling traffic back to region A using 10/30/60% ramps.

Scenario B: Dedicated tenant X hitting OOMs on private model variant
- Detection: tenant-specific OOM alerts; logs show KV cache pressure.
- Immediate mitigations: restart runtime with reduced KV cache, enable smaller-model fallback if tenant contract allows, enter short throttle mode for non-critical routes.
- If overflow allowed: route non-critical requests to shared overflow with strict data-tagging to anonymize payloads per contract.
- Postmortem focus: GC/allocator tuning, model compilation flags (fp16/8), consider adding burst capacity to tenant commit.

Decision heuristics and metrics to drive routing choices
- Latency tail (P95/P99) per region and tenant.
- Cost delta between variants (tokens * per-token-cost). Treat cost as secondary to SLA for platinum customers.
- Data residency constraints (binary allow/deny).
- Model compatibility score: a small compatibility mismatch may increase hallucination risk; models with high risk should not be used for safety-critical tenants.

API-level flags and per-tenant settings to expose
- allow_cross_region_egress: true/false
- allow_variant_spillover_to_shared_pools: true/false
- prefer_latency_over_cost: true/false
- max_allowed_variant_degradation: low/medium/high (human readable setting mapped to thresholds)

Runbook templates for oncall (short)
1) Triage: Confirm alert scope (tenant vs global).
2) Lock-in: If Private or Dedicated and tenant-scoped, do containment actions only.
3) Execute fallback: following decision order above; document chosen fallback in incident ticket.
4) Monitor: watch P50/P95/P99 and token-cost.
5) Rollback: re-route traffic back using phased ramp and run integration checks.
6) Post-incident: capture root cause and update router heuristics if needed.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups
- How to handle telemetry gaps for Private deployments where observability is limited? Proposal: lightweight heartbeat webhook that customers opt-in to at onboarding; platform gives reduced heuristics when absent.
- Billing semantics during cross-region failover for Hosted customers: do we bill at origin-region rates or execution-region rates? Need finance and product decision.
- Policy edge-cases: tenants with partial privacy constraints (only embeddings can egress across region). Need finer-grained per-route egress policies.

Appendix: quick checklist for onboarding team
- Capture egress policy during onboarding and store as tenant metadata.
- Default opt-outs: do not enable cross-cloud failover unless explicitly requested.
- Provide a one-click opt-in for "shared-overflow" for Dedicated with clear SLA and logging terms.
- Ensure bundle of control-plane runbooks is included with Dedicated and Private SOWs.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Run simulation of regional failover using synthetic traffic generator and measure rollback ramp safety. (Marcus)
- Draft a clear billing proposal for cross-region execution pricing and pass to finance. (Renee)
- Prototype heartbeat webhook for Private customers and measure adoption friction. (Tomás)

End of note
